preamble: A nasalized front mid vowel lowers to the open nasal [ã]. Nasality makes vowel-height contrasts harder to perceive, so mid nasal vowels tend to lower and merge with open ones. In French, Old French [ẽ] (from e before a nasal) lowered through [æ̃] and merged with [ã] in the 11th to early 12th century. That merger is why en and an are pronounced alike today (dent = dans [dɑ̃]). In Old Polish, the front nasal *ę and the back nasal *ǫ merged into a single nasal vowel of [ã] quality. The two were redistributed by length only in the 15th and 16th centuries.

examples.note: Nasal [ẽ] lowered through [æ̃] to [ã], probably during the 11th or early 12th century, and merged with the reflex of Latin an. Later [ã] backed to [ɑ̃].
Now a homophone of vend 'sells' and identical in vowel to vante; the en/an merger was complete in Central French.

In Old Polish the front and back nasals merged in quality into a single nasal [ã], while length still contrasted. The long vowel later developed into ą and the short one into ę, which gives the alternation pięć 'five' (old short) ~ piąty 'fifth' (old long).
